# Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? Rigorous Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code Generation

**EvalPlus** · NeurIPS 2023 (per the v3 PDF footer, p. 1)

Read: [PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.01210) · [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210)  
Code: [evalplus](https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus)

<p class="notice">An AI-written summary for orientation, not a source: check the original paper before relying on anything here.</p>

## In brief

- Augments code benchmarks with generated tests (HumanEval+: 80× the tests of HumanEval) (abstract).
- Re-evaluates 26 LLMs and finds the original tests too weak (abstract).
- Weak tests inflating code-generation scores.

## In plain words

Code-writing LLMs are scored by running their programs on a benchmark's hand-written tests, and the authors argue these tests "can be limited in both quantity and quality" (abstract), so wrong code can pass, "leading to false confidence in the results" (§1, Fig. 1). They build EvalPlus, which adds many generated test inputs to an existing benchmark: ChatGPT writes starting inputs, small random changes that respect each input's data type multiply them, and each LLM program's output is compared with the task's reference solution's (§2). Applied to HumanEval, a popular set of 164 Python tasks, it gives HumanEval+ with 80× the tests (abstract). Across 26 LLMs, pass@k (the estimated chance that at least one of k sampled programs passes) is up to 19.3–28.9% lower than on the original tests, depending on k (abstract, §1). With one greedy-decoded program per task, two open 34B code models that were "no better than ChatGPT" on HumanEval "can actually outperform" it on HumanEval+ (§3). The authors say they "are the first to study the test inadequacy problem in current programming benchmarks" (§1).

## Background and terms

**Terms to know:** [pass@k](#/glossary/passk) · [differential testing](#/glossary/differential-testing) · [test oracle](#/glossary/test-oracle) · [fuzzing](#/glossary/fuzzing) · [mutation testing](#/glossary/mutation-testing) · [branch and path coverage](#/glossary/branch-and-path-coverage) · [set cover problem](#/glossary/set-cover-problem) (the authors say finding a minimal subset of tests "is equivalent to the set covering problem" and run "a greedy set cover algorithm", §2.2, §1) · [programming by contract](#/glossary/programming-by-contract) (applied to preconditions, as assertions, §2.3) · [translation validation](#/glossary/translation-validation) (named as a verification method for domain-specific problems, §1, and as future work, §5)

**The paper's own terms:**
- **HumanEval**: "164 human-written programming tasks", each giving the LLM a Python function signature and a docstring; a solution is judged by "a handful of manual test-cases" (§3 "Setup", Tab. 2).
- **HumanEval+**: HumanEval with the generated tests added and its incorrect reference solutions fixed (§3 "Setup"). In Tab. 3 its rows are "+extra"; the original's are "base".
- **HumanEval+-mini**: HumanEval+ cut down by test-suite reduction, "as an option to speed up evaluation" (§3 "Setup").
- **ground truth**: a task's reference solution, the oracle LLM output is compared against (§2). For HumanEval+ the authors "carefully re-implemented and tested all ground-truths" (§3 "Setup").
- **pass@1⋆ and the sampled pass@k**: pass@1⋆ scores one greedy-decoded program per task. The sampled pass@k (k = 1, 10, 100) uses 200 programs per task at each of four temperatures and reports the best temperature for each k (§3 "Setup", Tab. 3). By default both are run; GPT-4 gets greedy decoding only, and ChatGPT greedy plus temperature 0.8 only, "due to time and cost constraints" (§3 "Setup").
- **type-aware mutation**: making a new input from a seed by changing it according to its data type; for example, numbers move up or down by one, and items or substrings of lists, strings and dictionaries are removed, repeated or replaced, recursively by their inner types (§2.1 "Type-aware input mutation", Tab. 1). An "ingredient mechanism" collects data fragments already seen and reuses them (§2.1).
- **program input contracts**: hand-written assertions on a function's preconditions ("e.g., assert n > 0") that can filter out invalid generated inputs and clarify the prompt (§2.3).
- **test-suite reduction**: choosing a subset of tests that still meets every testing requirement the full suite meets (§2.2).
- **sample killings**: the wrong LLM programs a test catches, a testing requirement for reduction; under leave-one-out, a model's own programs are left out when its suite is built (§2.2 "LLM sample killings", §3).

**Builds on:**
- HumanEval and the unbiased pass@k estimator of Chen et al. [11] (§3 "Setup"; not listed here).
- Differential testing, McKeeman [40], as the oracle (§1, §2; not listed here).
- The mutation-based fuzzing workflow of the fuzzers AFL and libFuzzer [74, 57], and type-aware mutation from Winterer et al. [66] (§2.1; not listed here).
- Test-suite reduction [75, 59] and mutation testing [7] (§2.2; not listed here).

## Problem and setting

- **Question:** "Is the code generated by LLMs really correct?" (§1). The authors name two weaknesses of benchmarks: insufficient testing and imprecise problem descriptions (§1).
- **What "correct" means:** a program "is regarded to be correct if for all test inputs it returns values that match the expected outputs within a reasonable run time" (App. A "Test oracles"): exact match by default, floats within the tolerance HumanEval annotates or 10⁻⁶, and a per-test timeout of the larger of 200 ms and four times the ground truth's run time (App. A).
- **Benchmark:** "While EvalPlus is general", the paper "focuses on evaluating its effectiveness on" HumanEval (§3 "Setup").
- **Models:** 26 LLMs, code-specialized and general-purpose, open and commercial (Tab. 5, App. A).
- **Generation budget:** per task, around 30 ChatGPT seed inputs from 3 prompts, then type-aware mutation for 1000 additional inputs within a one-hour budget (§3 "Setup"). 83 of the 164 tasks carry hand-written contracts (§3 "Setup").

## Approach

The pipeline (Fig. 2, §2):
- **Seed inputs from ChatGPT (§2.1):** each prompt holds the ground truth, sampled existing test inputs and one instruction (for complex, difficult or corner-case inputs, Fig. 2). The authors say ChatGPT can generate inputs "valid even under semantic constraints", such as a palindrome (§2.1). Inputs violating the ground truth's precondition are filtered out.
- **Type-aware mutation (§2.1, Tab. 1):** a fuzzing loop picks a random input from the seed pool, mutates it by type, and adds the result to the pool if it meets the contract.
- **Oracle (§2):** differential testing of each LLM program against the ground truth on all inputs.
- **Optional reduction (§2.2):** greedy set cover over branches covered, mutants of the ground truth killed, or wrong LLM programs caught (leave-one-out), or all three together.

## Results

- **Scale (§3 "Setup", Tab. 2):** HumanEval+ has 80× HumanEval's tests; HumanEval+-mini is 47× smaller than HumanEval+ (§3 "Effectiveness of test-suite reduction").
- **Scores drop (§3 "Evaluation of LLMs", Tab. 3):** "almost all pass@k results consistently drop" across models, sizes and k, with maximum reductions of up to 19.3–28.9% for different k (abstract, §1). For GPT-4, greedy pass@1 goes from 88.4 on HumanEval to 76.2 on HumanEval+ (Tab. 3).
- **Rankings change (§3, Tab. 3):** WizardCoder-CodeLlama and Phind-CodeLlama (34B open code models, Tab. 5) were "no better than ChatGPT" on HumanEval in pass@1⋆ and "can actually outperform" it on HumanEval+. HumanEval+ also gives other "contrary examples", such as SantaCoder-1B over InCoder-6.7B and Vicuna-7B over InCoder-1.3B (open code models; Vicuna is general-purpose, Tab. 5).
- **Temperature (§3, Tab. 3):** optimal temperatures "seem to stay fairly consistent" before and after HumanEval+, with slight differences.
- **Reduced suite (§3 "Effectiveness of test-suite reduction", Tab. 4):** under leave-one-out on a subset of models, the combined reduction "can achieve almost the same pass@1⋆ drop" as HumanEval+ with 47× fewer tests. Set covering over each metric alone "can harness the pass@1⋆ of the base" HumanEval "to certain degree"; sample killings are "the most effective, leading to the same effectiveness as the full approach", but use "more tests than other theoretical metrics".
- **Per-task pass rates (§3 "Pass rate distribution", Fig. 3):** "overall" HumanEval+ can detect misjudged solutions for problems "of all levels of difficulties".
- **Faulty HumanEval ground truths (§3 "Incorrect 'ground-truth' in HumanEval", Fig. 4):** 18 defects (11% of problems): 5 unhandled edge cases, 10 bad logic, 3 performance issues, found by differential testing between the original and the re-implemented ground truths. Fig. 4 shows an operator-precedence bug in task #124 that no base test exposes.

## Limits the authors state

- "Ideally, we would like to formally verify the correctness of LLM-provided solutions for any input", but verifying even domain-specific problems is "already challenging enough", so benchmarks rely on tests (§1).
- ChatGPT "is unsuitable for large amounts of automated test generation due to undesired speed and cost of querying such a large model" (§2.1).
- With many generated tests, "the test execution can be costly" (§2.2).
- For reduction by sample killings, "for a new LLM under evaluation, we do not have any test execution results for its code samples" (§2.2), hence leave-one-out.
- GPT-4 and ChatGPT are evaluated in fewer decoding settings "due to time and cost constraints" (§3 "Setup").
- Tab. 4 covers "a subset of representative models" because of time and space constraints (§3 "Effectiveness of test-suite reduction").

## Open problems and building blocks

  - Apply EvalPlus to "more code benchmarks such as MBPP" (§5), a crowd-sourced Python benchmark with three tests per problem (§4 "Coding benchmark for LLMs").
  - Integrate EvalPlus "with more formal verification (e.g., Dafny [32]) or validation techniques (e.g., translation validation [36]) to provide stronger guarantees of the evaluation results when applicable" (§5); Dafny is a program verifier [32].
  - "look more closely on the effect of temperature with respect to the robustness of the evaluation tests" (§3).
  - Tasks with multiple conditions, completeness, reasoning or efficiency requirements are the hardest for the evaluated LLMs, "positioning future research to improve LLMs for conquering such coding skills" (§3 "Pass rate distribution").
- **Released:** "We have open-sourced our tools, enhanced datasets as well as all LLM-generated code" (abstract); a PyPI package and a leaderboard of newly evaluated models (§5).
- **To reuse it:** a correct ground truth per task, since EvalPlus "requires ground-truth solutions to cross-check LLM-generated code" (§3 "Setup"); ChatGPT for seeds (§2.1); hand-written contracts to keep inputs well-formed (§2.3); mutations for the Python types of Tab. 1; other models' programs for reduction by sample killings (§2.2).
- **Beyond its domain:** the test generation technique "can be even used to remind developers of potential flaws of the accepted LLM-generated code snippets when doing AI pair-programming" (§5), e.g. with Copilot, GitHub's coding assistant [42].
